title: RIP Margaret Hamilton, whose code saved the Apollo 11 Moon landing
gist: Obituary of Margaret Hamilton, who coined 'software engineering' and led Apollo onboard flight software; her priority-scheduling failsafe let Apollo 11 land despite computer overload alarms. Its lessons on fault tolerance and error prevention underlie her later companies.

insights.claim: Margaret Hamilton, who coined the term 'software engineering' and led Apollo onboard flight software development, died at age 90.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Marks the passing of a founder of the software-reliability discipline.

insights.claim: Hamilton's priority-display failsafe let the Apollo 11 computer shed nonessential tasks during overload, preventing an abort of the Moon landing.
insights.speaker: Margaret Hamilton
insights.so_what: Classic case for graceful degradation design in mission-critical systems.
insights.quote: If the computer hadn’t recognized this problem and taken recovery action, I doubt if Apollo 11 would have been the successful Moon landing it was.

insights.claim: NASA initially rejected Hamilton's proposed safeguard against the 'P01' error found by her daughter, until astronaut Jim Lovell made that error on Apollo 8 and erased navigation data.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Illustrates the cost of dismissing user-error edge cases in critical software.

insights.claim: Hamilton founded Higher Order Software in 1976 and Hamilton Technologies in 1985, whose Universal Systems Language focused on error prevention and defensive programming.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Lineage of formal, error-preventing software methods.

insights.claim: Hamilton programmed Edward Lorenz's LGP-30 weather simulations at MIT, the work behind the discovery of sensitivity to initial conditions in chaos theory.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Historical context for computation's role in science.
insights.locator: She ended up working for Edward Lorenz

insights.claim: Apollo software was stored in core rope memory woven by New England textile workers, earning Hamilton the nickname 'rope mother'.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
